    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

    Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
    • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
    • It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

    At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

    It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

    The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

    “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

    When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

    Industry observers note that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

    It has been revealed that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

    It has been revealed that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” claims Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

    As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

    Industry observers note that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

    Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

    The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

    In a recent development, if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

    According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team demonstrated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

    In a recent development, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

    Sources indicate that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

    This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

    Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

    It has been revealed that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga claims, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

    About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

    In a recent development, dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

    According to recent reports, but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

    Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

    Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics organization XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

    Recent findings suggest that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

    Recent findings suggest that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

    Industry observers note that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

    After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

    In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

    Sources indicate that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

    In a recent development, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga notes.

    Recent findings suggest that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

    But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more notable than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell notes. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

    In a recent development, during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

    Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

    According to recent reports, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

    Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

    And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu states.

    Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

    “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

    Recent findings suggest that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra claims, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

    “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra notes. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

    If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

    In a recent development, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

    Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

    It has been revealed that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

    In a recent development, the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as rapidly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

    It has been revealed that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

    A few months after my visit, Remedy unveiled US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

    Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

    The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

    Sources indicate that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person firm into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every time news comes out about the French video game publisher/developer Ubisoft, it’s either something gamers are pleasantly surprised by or something entirely negative that doesn’t come as a shock.
    • In a recent development, it was nice to learn that studio franchises like Assassin’s Creed, The Division and Rayman were either getting content expansions or new series installments altogether.
    • After releasing its latest earnings report, Ubisoft has confirmed its intentions to go all-in on incorporating generative AI technologies into video game development with a latest studio.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every time news comes out about the French video game publisher/developer Ubisoft, it’s either something gamers are pleasantly surprised by or something entirely negative that doesn’t come as a shock.

    In a recent development, it was nice to learn that studio franchises like Assassin’s Creed, The Division and Rayman were either getting content expansions or new series installments altogether. But it was equally disappointing to learn about the 2026 cancellation of several in-development projects, including the troubled remake of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. Gamers were ecstatic to hear that Ubisoft halted any future development in NFTs and Web3 gaming. But now they’ll probably be less than enthused all over again, now that Ubisoft is shifting its next big tech focus to generative AI.

    After releasing its latest earnings report, Ubisoft has confirmed its intentions to go all-in on incorporating generative AI technologies into video game development with a latest studio. But with that news comes the tech giant’s latest round of layoffs, which resulted in hundreds of its studio’s game developers losing their roles at Ubisoft.

    With both events happening so close to each other, it’s easy to see why gamers are questioning Ubisoft’s latest moves.

    Ubisoft made it known that they’re making a big move towards playable generative AI experiences when it highlighted the newly introduced in-house studio behind its efforts in its most recent earnings report.

    It has been revealed that “Motherbrain, the team behind Teammates, the Group’s first playable generative AI experience, has been established as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technology for newly introduced forms of gameplay. Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds,” the company stated. “It aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft’s Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and form partnerships with selected technology actors.”.

    Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot commented on the creation of Motherbrain, noting that it is “the team behind our first playable generative AI experience Teammates, as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators and open up fresh possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences.”.

    Those experiences will focus on utilizing more intelligent non-playable characters with stronger memory and AI game masters that properly manage large-scale in-game worlds.

    According to recent reports, motherbrain’s Teammates has been in development for a good while now and was recently showcased to members of the gaming media in a playable state. The people who got their hands on it refer to it as an immersive first-person shooter where players are joined by two robotic AI companions that they can order around by issuing real-time voice commands.

    The game’s narrative director, Virginie Mosser, looked to ease the fears of gamers who are wary of generative AI being implemented in video games and AI tools being used to make them.

    “At first, I had the same concerns as many others,” Mosser noted. “But I discovered that it’s the exact opposite of removing the human from the process. I still write the story and character personalities, but instead of fixed lines, we create these kinds of fences that let NPCs improvise within the world but stay within the boundaries of the lore and motivations we have given them. They can improvise, but we still set the rules and direct the story and characters.”.

    Recent findings suggest that gamers still have reason to give Ubisoft the side eye about its big generative AI video game development plans, especially since the tech giant was so quick to abandon its trend-chasing foray into the world of NFTs and Web3 gaming. The most recent round of layoffs at the company, which resulted in the loss of 166 roles from its Montreal and Quebec studios, has also given gamers another reason to be skeptical about Ubisoft’s AI game-making initiative.

    Even though Ubisoft enacted these layoffs “to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs,” it’s not out of the realm of possibility to question its true motives for its latest job cuts.

    It has been revealed that has Ubisoft decided to pour major investments into generative AI game development at the cost of sacrificing its human talent? Will more layoffs occur in the near future as the tech giant strengthens its AI game development efforts? Can gamers expect to hear about more AI tool usage implemented in the creation of future entries in Ubisoft’s biggest franchises? And if Motherbrain’s Teammates bombs, will Ubisoft promptly leave generative AI video game development behind and go on to the next significant tech fad?

    As someone who’s always chatting with gamers and critics who cover the medium, I always hear how they could do without any sort of AI being utilized in the video game creation process. And they especially don’t want to hear AI voices emanating from their favorite games and replacing human ones.

    It has been revealed that that last sentiment is evidenced by the overwhelmingly negative reactions to Embark Studios (the development studio behind The Finals) replacing its human esports broadcasters with in-game AI commentators. Ubisoft has experienced some major ups and downs as of late—their major bet on generative AI game development has a high chance of producing another loss if their latest endeavors don’t work as well as intended.

    In a recent development, in the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics. Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture. From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 concern of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine:.

    In a recent development, feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I remarked to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”.

    John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well:.

    Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

    Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine, rubber bands, how trains go around curves, and magnets. Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets, he notes:.

    I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

    Feynman was also quoted as saying:.

    I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

    Recent findings suggest that pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:.

    What I cannot create, I do not understand.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

    Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

    But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

    And in iOS 27, Apple added a latest setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

    While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

    Fresh in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

    Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

    You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

    This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

    Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

    Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations

    • This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L.
    • Sources indicate that the statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

    Sources indicate that the statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/. Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean, names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

    The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.

    Industry observers note that the formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper notes that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

    The source of the paper is not in this repository.

    Recent findings suggest that the package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

    Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Wiley

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places.
    • Recent findings suggest that this shift changes how devices are designed.
    • This White Paper explains these challenges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

    Recent findings suggest that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

    In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:.

    His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving consumers more control over lighting and depth of field. The manufacturer also introduced a customizable Camera app interface with professional controls.

    Industry observers note that bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report notes.

    McCormack spoke in depth about iOS 27 features like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing in an interview with Tyler Stalman in June. He emphasized how the features “preserve the integrity of the moment.”.

    Pavel Durov speaks at TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in Berlin in October 2013.

    Telegram CEO Pavel Durov mocked Apple’s iPhone Duo on X, calling it “both too massive and too small“, while announcing that Telegram now supports the foldable. The app switches to a two-column layout when the phone is opened.

    Telegram has adapted its app for Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and its CEO used the moment to mock the device. “Apple finally made a phone that’s both too massive and too small,” Pavel Durov wrote on X on Thursday.

    Industry observers note that “It folds in half. Just like your enthusiasm,” he added.

    Durov remarked Telegram still looked “incredible at both wrong sizes,” and joked that the firm does “a lot of charity work.” He shared a short video of the app running on the foldable.

    Sources indicate that when the phone is closed, Telegram looks like its usual iPhone version, Brazilian Apple site MacMagazine reported. Opened, it switches to a two-column layout like the iPad app, with chats on one side and the conversation on the other.

    The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner one. It sold out in minutes when preorders opened in October.

    Industry observers note that reviewers praised the hinge but noted that many apps still needed updates for the bigger screen. Instagram chief Adam Mosseri said this week that designing for the Duo will be hard.

    According to recent reports, durov has clashed with Apple before. In August, Apple briefly pulled Telegram from the App Store over a content violation. Durov remarked extortionists had found a way “to manipulate [Apple] into overreacting.”.

    Recent findings suggest that I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

    Industry observers note that it was my secret in my student days that my looks were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe.

    Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:.

    How do you descend from a state of pure exaltation?

    What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.

    The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and controlled by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by his power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning grandeur—that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”.

    Rand’s essay states: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

    There’s a mural by Diego Rivera I love. It’s called Man, Controller of the Universe:.

    It has been revealed that it’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.

    Industry observers note that and I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!

    And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read Machines of Loving Grace: humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word!

    Industry observers note that it’s a betrayal and a surrender. Man is a bridge, a rusty old bridge that we can neither preserve nor restore. We can move forward and become as the gods, or retreat back into the caves. And the dream of the AI companies, and of most people in AI safety and effective altruism and rationalism; is instead that we should lie down in a warm bath, watch the demons we summoned dance in the sky, and slip away.     #28042. Valkey kills the skiplist, cuts sorted set overhead by up to 43%

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1508 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Valkey ↗ Open Full Page

    Valkey kills the skiplist, cuts sorted set overhead by up to 43%

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Valkey

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.
    • In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree.
    • It has been revealed that fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.

    In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree.

    It has been revealed that fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. In a 5-million-member test, it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36–43%, saving up to 109 MB.

    Let's take a look at why this change happened and how it works.

    In a recent development, large sorted sets that exceed the listpack threshold are backed by a skiplist paired with a hashtable (smaller sorted sets use a compact listpack representation that stores elements sequentially in contiguous memory). The hashtable gives O(1) lookups by member, while the skiplist gives O(log n) ordered lookups by rank or score. That pairing is architecturally simple, but the skiplist carries a significant memory cost. It stores exactly one element per node, scattered across memory as separate allocations connected by pointers.

    Valkey's skiplist pays for this in raw memory. Every node carries a backward pointer (8B), plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, since skiplists are probabilistic (each node has a 25% chance of gaining another level). Each level costs 8B for the pointer plus 8B for the span value, giving around 29B of pointer and span overhead per node. Add the 8B score, and the total reaches roughly 37B per node before accounting for the member string.

    Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of hardware caches (L1, L2, and L3) to keep frequently accessed data close to the processor. These caches are much smaller and faster than main memory (RAM), so when the CPU cannot find the data it needs in its cache, it must fetch it from a slower level of the memory hierarchy. As a rough illustration, an L1 cache hit can take about 1 ns, while a DRAM access can take around 100 ns. A dependent memory access can leave the core waiting; actual latency and how much work can be hidden vary by system and workload 1.

    Each node in the skiplist is a separate allocation, potentially scattered wherever the heap happened to place it, so following the structure can require repeatedly fetching data from unrelated memory locations. Because each step can determine where the next step goes, these fetches are dependent, resulting in more round trips through the memory hierarchy. A 2025 study of concurrent in-memory indexes found that, on its tested workloads, traditional skiplists experienced roughly 2.4–4.8× more cache misses than a comparable B-tree, with 2–8× lower throughput 2 (testing different data structure implementations, not Valkey).

    A B+ tree keeps entries sorted in fixed-size nodes: leaf nodes hold the entries, or pointers to them, and inner nodes hold just enough routing data to pick which child to descend into. Packing many entries into each node addresses both problems above: far less per-member pointer overhead, and far fewer dependent fetches per lookup.

    According to recent reports, fbtree, short for Feature B+ Tree, uses a 61-way fanout: each node can hold up to 61 entries or child pointers. Leaf and inner nodes are sized to fit jemalloc allocation classes without wasting space on 64-bit builds; on supported 32-bit builds, innerNode is rounded up to the 1280-byte class.

    A 512-byte leaf holds up to 61 value pointers, so 61 members share one node instead of each getting its own. Instead of storing the score and member separately, fbtree stores them together as a single packed value: the normalized 8-byte score followed by the member bytes. This keeps the data needed for comparisons together and removes another level of pointer indirection.

    It has been revealed that the skiplist's 25%-per-level rule gives it an effective branching factor of about 4, while fbtree's fanout is 61. Both structures retain O(log n) search complexity, but the B+ tree has substantially fewer levels to traverse and therefore fewer opportunities for expensive memory fetches.

    A modern CPU can also fetch several adjacent cache lines efficiently when the data is laid out contiguously, thanks in part to the way memory is accessed and to hardware prefetching 1. Therefore a B+ tree node that spans a few cache lines can be read efficiently as the CPU scans its contents.

    On top of that structure, fbtree adds optimizations aimed at specific operations.

    In a recent development, in a B+ tree keyed by variable-length strings, such as sorted set members, picking a child means comparing the lookup against each child’s anchor, the largest member in that child, and reading those strings costs memory fetches. fbtree's inner nodes store each anchor along with a small four-byte "feature." Because the anchors often share a common prefix, fbtree stores that shared prefix separately and uses the four feature bytes to distinguish the children. The implementation can then compare those features in parallel using SIMD, often identifying the correct child before fetching the child node itself. If the features uniquely identify a child, the search can descend immediately; otherwise, they still narrow the range that needs a full binary search.

    Sources indicate that range commands such as ZRANGE walk the set in order. fbtree links its leaf nodes in a doubly-linked list, so a scan can move from leaf to leaf without climbing back up the tree. The skiplist requests an item, waits to receive it, and only knows the next item to fetch when it's received the first. The B+ tree can work on up to 61 items in parallel, and while it works on those it can fetch the next leaf node with the next 61 items.

    According to recent reports, commands such as ZPOPMIN work at the ends of the set. fbtree caches its leftmost and rightmost leaves, so finding them is O(1), as in a skiplist, instead of O(log n). This keeps pop and append operations at parity rather than regressing.

    Range deletions remove a contiguous run of members, and fbtree handles them without rebuilding the surrounding structure.

    The change is internal: sorted set commands and their behavior remain unchanged. The one visible difference is that OBJECT ENCODING returns btree instead of skiplist for a large sorted set. If you have monitoring, tests, or tooling that checks for the literal string skiplist, that's one place to enhancement. Small sorted sets under the listpack threshold are unaffected either way, since they never used the skiplist encoding to begin with.

    The numbers below compare only the ordered index: skiplist versus fbtree, with the hashtable and member embedding unchanged.

    Inserting 5 million 20-byte members sequentially reduced per-member memory overhead, excluding the member data itself, from 50.3B to 28.5B, a 43% reduction. The same 5 million members inserted in random order reduced per-member overhead from 50.3B to 32.0B, a 36% reduction.

    The smaller reduction comes from random insertion leaving more partially filled nodes than sequential insertion.

    Industry observers note that for the 5-million-member set in this test, that is roughly 109 MB saved with sequential inserts and 92 MB with random inserts. The savings are per member, not per byte stored, so the relative reduction in total memory is largest for sets with many small members and shrinks as member size grows.

    Industry observers note that the benchmarks below were measured on PR #4206’s oi/pr3-fbtree-v2 branch and were not rerun for the merged commit. They were run on a Graviton3 c7g.metal system with 64 cores, nine I/O threads, a pipeline depth of 10, and a 3-million-member sorted set. Each test was repeated five times; the reported confidence intervals were ≤2% for all commands except ZRANDMEMBER.

    The same underlying design changes also improve throughput for several sorted set operations:.

    ZADD and ZREM reposition elements in the tree, so they gain the most from fbtree's shallower structure and fewer pointer updates. Range operations see smaller gains because once the index traversal becomes cheap, producing and returning the requested elements becomes a larger part of the total cost. ZSCORE and ZRANDMEMBER barely move because they use the hashtable, not the ordered index.

    The important takeaway: the commands didn't change, but in our tests large sorted sets carried 36–43% less per-member overhead, and ZADD and ZREM throughput rose 105% and 76%.

    The goal wasn't simply to make the data structure faster in isolation: the implementation was repeatedly benchmarked against the existing skiplist through the full Valkey server, with optimizations added until fbtree matched or exceeded the skiplist across the tested sorted set commands.

    Valkey 9.2 is currently in release-candidate testing. Before GA, try the 9.2 release candidate with your real workload, especially if large sorted sets or commands such as ZADD, ZREM, ZRANK, or ZCOUNT are vital to you. Your testing and feedback can help surface challenges before the final release, so open an issue with anything you find.

    Tesla has started offering rides in its Cybercab in Dallas, the second city after Austin for the two-seater with no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla already runs Model Y robotaxis in Dallas and prepares to start delivering Cybercabs to private buyers in Texas in December.

    According to recent reports, tesla’s Cybercab, its two-seat robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals, is now giving rides in Dallas, InsideEVs reported. “Cybercab has arrived in your city,” Tesla’s Robotaxi account posted on X on Thursday.

    Dallas is the second city to get the Cybercab, after it began giving rides in Austin in September. Tesla already runs driverless Model Y robotaxis in Dallas. Riders book both in the Tesla Robotaxi app.

    Tesla’s robotaxis also run in Houston, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Tampa, Orlando and Miami, mostly with the Model Y. It has focused on Texas and Florida, where the rules are looser than in states like California.

    Sources indicate that the US road safety agency, NHTSA, is looking into how Tesla decided a car with no wheel or pedals meets US safety rules. Unlike Amazon’s Zoox, Tesla did not ask for an exemption. NHTSA is also reviewing claims that Tesla robotaxis, including Cybercabs, sped in school zones.

    Industry observers note that tesla is also starting to sell the Cybercab to some customers for $29,990. Owners must pay a $299 monthly fee, or the car will not run. The first cars should reach buyers in Texas in December.

    To build more of them, Tesla looks to wind down Cybertruck output at its Texas plant around mid-2027.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that not sure what to do with your time between waiting around for a delicious Thanksgiving feast and prepping for the holidays as they bear down on us? Paramount+ is a great streaming service for finding plenty to watch that you may not have seen before, especially after the platform recently loaded up its library with a mountain of additional catalog titles at the start of November. That means there’s plenty to dig into this weekend if you want something to cozy up to this holiday season.

    This week, I’ve pulled out three very different picks that have all found a home on the platform. You can revisit a beloved ’90s Nickelodeon classic that serves as a lovely showcase for the late Michelle Trachtenberg, or sink your teeth into a gloriously campy 2002 gothic horror cult favorite featuring one of Aaliyah’s final roles.

    Sources indicate that and if you're ready to kick off the holidays early, there’s also one of the all-time great seasonal comedies: Bill Murray’s wickedly funny spin on a classic Christmas story. Here are the three Paramount+ movies you need to be streaming this weekend, with one of my all-time favorites included.

    Tired of the same old, same old Christmas carols? This is a much different take and your official start to the season. Bill Murray is Frank Cross, a cynical TV executive so consumed by ratings and money that he thinks nothing of firing an employee days before Christmas. On Christmas Eve, as he preps a live broadcast of “A Christmas Carol,” Frank is visited by the ghost of his old mentor and then by three spirits of his own.

    Sources indicate that they drag him through his past, present and future in an attempt to change his ways. It’s sharp, mean, and weirdly poignant all at once, which is exactly what makes it perfect for the holidays, and well, anytime, really.

    Watch "Scrooged" on Paramount+ now.

    The first-ever Nickelodeon Movies production, “Harriet the Spy” is one of the smartest kids’ flicks of the ‘90s, and I should know. I lived it.

    In a recent development, michelle Trachtenberg is 11-year-old Harriet M. Welsch, an aspiring writer who prowls her New York City neighborhood jotting down observations about everyone she knows in a secret notebook. When a rival classmate gets hold of that notebook and reads its contents aloud to the whole school, Harriet’s unfiltered thoughts turn her friends and classmates against her. Then she has to figure out how to make things right. Rosie O’Donnell is her beloved nanny Golly, and even Eartha Kitt surprisingly turns up for a role she devours. It’s a bittersweet tribute to Trachtenberg, who died earlier this year.

    Whether you’re revisiting it or showing it to your own kids, it’s well worth the trip back and you’ll remember it all immediately, especially “cabbages and kings.”.

    Watch "Harriet the Spy" on Paramount+ now.

    Based on Anne Rice’s “Vampire Chronicles,” the 2002 horror film follows Lestat (Stuart Townsend), an ancient vampire who wakes from a long slumber and reinvents himself as a glam rock star.

    Sources indicate that his performances bring someone much more dangerous out, though: Akasha (Aaliyah), the long-dormant queen of all vampires, who rises with prepares to make Lestat her king and remake the world in blood. The film is remembered today largely as one of the final roles for Aaliyah, who died before the film’s release. She’s absolutely gorgeous, a magnetic presence as Akasha.

    Lower your expectations for high art and enjoy it for the gloriously goth guilty pleasure it is, especially for all the nu-metal.

    Watch "Queen of the Damned" on Paramount+ now.

    StepSecurity raises $20M as hackers target the tools developers use

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (393 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • StepSecurity’s graphic announcing its $20M Series A.
    • StepSecurity, a Seattle-area startup founded by two former Microsoft engineers, has raised a $20M Series A led by Elephant.
    • According to recent reports, stepSecurity, a Seattle-area security startup, has raised a $20M Series A led by Elephant, GeekWire reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    StepSecurity’s graphic announcing its $20M Series A.

    StepSecurity, a Seattle-area startup founded by two former Microsoft engineers, has raised a $20M Series A led by Elephant. It protects developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and build pipelines from attackers who plant malicious code in open-source software.

    According to recent reports, stepSecurity, a Seattle-area security startup, has raised a $20M Series A led by Elephant, GeekWire reported. Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures also put in money, taking its total to $23M.

    Industry observers note that the organization guards the places where software gets built, from developers’ laptops to the systems that test and ship code. Hackers now often hide bad code in free, open-source software. Once it runs, it can steal passwords and keys.

    In a recent development, “A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team. Now one person can vibe code it,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post.

    In a recent development, the round landed in a busy week. On 17 November, hackers posted two poisoned versions of agent-framework, Microsoft’s Python toolkit for AI agents, which gets nearly 200,000 downloads a month. StepSecurity was among the firms that spotted the code, which stole passwords and keys, BleepingComputer reported.

    Recent findings suggest that tools for coders have been behind other big hacks. Binance notes its $6.3B hack started with a fake job interview and a tampered developer tool. Last month, a tampered Claude Code extension reached up to 5,000 Cursor people.

    Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft. Co-founder Ashish Kurmi also worked there before leading security at Uber and Plaid. They started StepSecurity in 2021 after living through the SolarWinds and Codecov attacks.

    Recent findings suggest that more than 20,000 open-source projects use its free tool, Harden-Runner. Its researchers also helped track the ChainDrop npm worm in August. StepSecurity states its yearly revenue grew fivefold in both 2024 and 2025, but gave no figures.

    Recent findings suggest that next, it prepares to guard the sandboxes where AI agents run code. Worms such as Miasma already target AI coding tools. Rivals are growing too: Belgium’s Aikido became a $1B unicorn in January.
